title: Limits & Continuity
description: What happens as we approach a value?

concepts.title: What is a Limit?
concepts.contentHtml:
A limit describes what value a function approaches as its input gets closer and closer to some number.

Think of it like walking toward a door -- the limit is what's on the other side, even if you never actually step through.

We write it as:

concepts.title: Left and Right Limits
concepts.contentHtml:
Sometimes a function approaches different values depending on which direction you come from.

The left-hand limit is what happens as you approach from below (from the left on the number line). The right-hand limit is from above.

A limit only exists if both sides agree!

concepts.title: Continuity
concepts.contentHtml:
A function is continuous at a point if you can draw it without lifting your pen.

More precisely, f(x) is continuous at x = a when three things are true:

1. f(a) exists (the function is defined there)
2. The limit as x approaches a exists
3. The limit equals f(a)

If any of these fail, we have a discontinuity -- a break, hole, or jump in the graph.

concepts.title: Slope of the Tangent Line
concepts.contentHtml:
The derivative measures how fast a function is changing at any point.

Imagine zooming in on a curve until it looks like a straight line. The slope of that line is the derivative.

We find it by taking two points on the curve, drawing a line between them (a secant line), then sliding the points closer and closer together.

concepts.title: The Power Rule
concepts.contentHtml:
The most useful derivative rule: for any power of x, bring the exponent down as a multiplier and reduce the power by one.

Examples:

x³ becomes 3x²
x⁵ becomes 5x⁴
x¹ becomes 1 (which is just 1)
x² becomes 2x

This simple pattern handles a huge number of functions!

concepts.title: Derivative as a Function
concepts.contentHtml:
The derivative itself is a new function -- it tells you the slope at every point.

If f(x) = x², then f'(x) = 2x. This means:

At x = 1, the slope is 2
At x = 3, the slope is 6
At x = -2, the slope is -4

Where the derivative is positive, the original function is increasing. Where it's negative, the function is decreasing. Where it's zero, we might have a peak or valley.

concepts.title: Area Under a Curve
concepts.contentHtml:
How do you find the area of a shape with curved edges? You can't just use length × width.

The key idea: fill the area with rectangles. The more rectangles you use, the better the approximation. These are called Riemann sums.

As the number of rectangles approaches infinity, the sum approaches the exact area. This is the integral.

concepts.title: Definite vs Indefinite Integrals
concepts.contentHtml:
A definite integral has bounds (from a to b) and gives you a number -- the area.

An indefinite integral has no bounds and gives you a function -- the antiderivative. It answers: "What function has this as its derivative?"

Don't forget the + C! Since the derivative of any constant is zero, there are infinitely many antiderivatives.

concepts.title: The Fundamental Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus is one of the most beautiful results in mathematics. It says:

Differentiation and integration are opposites.

If you integrate a function then differentiate the result, you get back to where you started. This connects the two main ideas of calculus into one unified theory.

concepts.title: Optimization
concepts.contentHtml:
One of the most practical uses of calculus: finding the maximum or minimum of a quantity.

The recipe:
1. Write the quantity to optimize as a function
2. Take its derivative
3. Set the derivative equal to zero and solve
4. Check which solutions are maxima vs minima

This works because at a peak or valley, the slope is flat (zero).

concepts.title: Related Rates
concepts.contentHtml:
When two quantities are related and both changing over time, calculus lets us connect their rates of change.

Classic example: a balloon inflating. The radius is growing at some rate. How fast is the volume growing?

Since V = (4/3)πr³, we differentiate both sides with respect to time and substitute the known rate.

concepts.title: Why Calculus Matters
concepts.contentHtml:
Calculus is the language of change, and change is everywhere:

Physics: velocity, acceleration, forces
Biology: population growth, spread of disease
Economics: marginal cost, optimization of profit
Engineering: signal processing, structural analysis
Machine Learning: gradient descent (training neural networks!)

Every time something changes smoothly, calculus is the tool to analyze it.

title: Chain Rule & Product Rule
description: Derivatives of composed and multiplied functions

concepts.title: The Product Rule
concepts.contentHtml:
When two functions are multiplied together, the derivative isn't just the product of their derivatives. Instead:

"First times derivative of second, plus second times derivative of first."

Example: d/dx [x² · sin(x)] = x² cos(x) + 2x sin(x)

Intuitively: both factors are changing simultaneously, and each contributes to the total rate of change.

concepts.title: The Chain Rule
concepts.contentHtml:
The chain rule handles nested functions — a function inside another function.

Think of it as peeling an onion: differentiate the outer layer, then multiply by the derivative of the inner layer.

Example: d/dx [sin(x²)] = cos(x²) · 2x

This is arguably the most important derivative rule. It appears everywhere in multivariable calculus and machine learning (backpropagation is repeated application of the chain rule!).

concepts.title: The Quotient Rule
concepts.contentHtml:
For a fraction of two functions, the quotient rule gives:

"Low d-high minus high d-low, all over the square of what's below."

Many students just rewrite f/g as f · g⁻¹ and use the product + chain rules instead. Both approaches give the same answer.

concepts.title: Polynomial Approximation
concepts.contentHtml:
Polynomials are easy to compute — just addition and multiplication. What if we could approximate any function using a polynomial?

That's exactly what a Taylor series does. Around a point a, we build a polynomial that matches the function's value, slope, curvature, and higher derivatives at that point.

The more terms we include, the better the approximation over a wider range.

concepts.title: Famous Taylor Series
concepts.contentHtml:
Some Taylor series are so important they're worth memorizing:

eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + … (converges everywhere!)

sin(x) = x - x³/3! + x⁵/5! - … (only odd powers)

cos(x) = 1 - x²/2! + x⁴/4! - … (only even powers)

1/(1-x) = 1 + x + x² + x³ + … (geometric series, |x| < 1)

concepts.title: Convergence & Euler's Identity
concepts.contentHtml:
A Taylor series may converge (give the correct value) only within a certain radius of convergence.

The geometric series 1/(1-x) only converges for |x| < 1. But eˣ, sin, and cos converge for all x.

The ultimate payoff: combining the series for eˣ, sin, and cos with imaginary numbers gives Euler's identity, often called the most beautiful equation in mathematics.

concepts.title: What is a Differential Equation?
concepts.contentHtml:
A differential equation (DE) is an equation that involves a function and its derivatives.

Instead of solving for a number, you solve for a function.

Example: dy/dx = 2x. What function has derivative 2x? Answer: y = x² + C.

DEs model everything from population growth to radioactive decay to the motion of planets.

concepts.title: Separation of Variables
concepts.contentHtml:
The simplest technique: if you can get all the y's on one side and all the x's on the other, you can integrate both sides separately.

Example: dy/dx = ky (exponential growth)

Separate: dy/y = k dx

Integrate: ln|y| = kx + C

Solve: y = Aeᵏˣ

This gives the exponential growth model — the solution to the simplest differential equation.

concepts.title: Second-Order & Oscillation
concepts.contentHtml:
A second-order DE involves the second derivative. The most famous one describes a spring:

y'' = -ω²y

"Acceleration is proportional to displacement but opposite in direction." The solution is sinusoidal oscillation: y = A cos(ωt) + B sin(ωt).

This single equation explains pendulums, vibrating strings, AC circuits, and even quantum wavefunctions.
mathExpressions: y'' + \omega^2 y = 0 \implies y = A\cos(\omega t) + B\sin(\omega t)

concepts.title: Partial Derivatives
concepts.contentHtml:
When a function has multiple inputs, like f(x, y) = x²y + 3y, we can take a derivative with respect to one variable while holding the others constant.

∂f/∂x treats y as a constant and differentiates with respect to x.

∂f/∂y treats x as a constant and differentiates with respect to y.

For f(x,y) = x²y + 3y: ∂f/∂x = 2xy, ∂f/∂y = x² + 3.

concepts.title: The Gradient
concepts.contentHtml:
The gradient collects all partial derivatives into a vector. It points in the direction of steepest ascent.

For f(x,y): ∇f = (∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y)

This is the foundation of gradient descent in machine learning: to minimize a loss function, you move in the direction opposite to the gradient.

The gradient's magnitude tells you how steep the hill is.

concepts.title: Multiple Integrals & Beyond
concepts.contentHtml:
Just as single integrals find area under curves, double integrals find volume under surfaces, and triple integrals find hypervolume.

The major theorems of multivariable calculus — Green's, Stokes', and the Divergence theorem — all generalize the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to higher dimensions.

They connect integrals over regions to integrals over their boundaries, and are essential in physics and engineering.
